text:
The two-story fishery management concept has been employed in recent years in a number of reservoirs in the southeastern United States. In such reservoirs, habitat is available throughout the year for both warmwater and coldwater fish. During the summer months, the coldwater habitat is maintained by thermal stratification of the reservoir water into layers. The coldwater fish habitat has an upper temperature limit and a lower dissolved oxygen limit.
From 1972 through January 1976, 158,000 trout approximately 9-inches in length (133,000 rainbow trout, (Salmo gairdneri), and 25,000 brown trout, (Salmo trutta)) have been stocked in Lake Jocassee. Threadfin shad (Dorosoma petenense) were introduced from 1972 through 1974 to serve as forage. The State presently plans continued trout releases on an annual basis to maintain a "put, grow, and take" trout fishery (Geddings, 1976).
Trout have been successfully introduced into Lake Jocassee, with large trout taken by fishermen. Studies of the Lake since 1974 revealed numerous 3- to 6-pound trout, with larger trout being caught since that time (up to 11 pounds). Lake Jocassee contains a promising trout fishery (Logan, 1976).
Growth of trout in Lake Jocassee has been estimated from returns of fish marked at stocking. Data for 28 trout caught in gill nets from August 13 to September 28, 1974 (Geddings, 1976), show calculated growth rates of 0.3 to 0.9 inches per month, averaging about 0.6 inch per month. Many of these fish had been stocked in February 1974. Data supplied by the Southeast Reservoir Investigations show growth rates for brown trout of about 5.4 to 7.9 inches per year (calculated average monthly growth rates of 0.4 to 0.7 inch). Growth is seasonal, with higher rates during spring and summer than during the rest of the year.
Gill netting samples have been taken for several years with data available since 1974. Southeast Reservoir Investigations (SERI) data (Table 2-8) show that in 1974 black crappie (Pomoxis nigromaculatus), largemouth bass, carp (Cyprinus carpio), flat bullhead (Ictalurus platycephalus), and quillback (Carpiodes cyprinus) dominated the samples, although brown trout and rainbow trout also appeared in significant numbers in the November samples. Samples for 1975-1976 were dominated by brown trout, along with black crappie, largemouth bass, quillback, carp, and flat bullhead.
